title: ビール大手を調査 経営層関与焦点
body:
缶ビールなどの出荷価格を巡ってカルテルを結んだ疑いが浮上し、公正取引委員会が７日、ビールメーカー大手４社に対する強制調査に乗り出した。激しい市場競争を演じてきた各社が、裏で話し合って価格を決めていた可能性が出ている。近年、価格カルテルの摘発に力を入れる公取委が今後、全容解明を図る。（小林岳人、奈良橋大輔）【グラフ】一目でわかる…ビールの店頭販売価格の推移
「まさに調査をスタートしたところだが、今回の事件の事実解明に全力投球していく」。７日の定例記者会見で、公取委の岩成博夫事務総長はそう強調した。
強制調査を受けたのは、アサヒビール、キリンビール、サントリー、サッポロビール（いずれも東京）。４社は遅くとも数年前から家庭用の缶ビールや発泡酒など、ビール類の出荷価格の値上げ幅や時期について、管理職クラスで話し合って決めていた疑いが持たれている。業界団体「ビール酒造組合」の定例会合「一木会」の後に各社幹部が集まるなどして情報交換をしていたとみられる。
ビールは、メーカーが決めた価格で卸売業者に出荷される。その後、スーパーやコンビニエンスストアなどの小売店などに流通するが、店頭での４社の主力商品は、ほぼ同価格帯で販売されることが多い。
３５０ミリ・リットル缶の店頭での想定価格は、アサヒの「スーパードライ」、キリンの「一番搾り」、サッポロの「黒ラベル」はそれぞれ２２８円前後、サントリーの「サントリー生ビール」は２１２円だ。小売り大手の関係者は「仕入れ価格も数円しか違わなく、ほとんどが横並びだ」と明かす。
２０２２年１０月と２５年４月には、原材料やエネルギー価格の高騰を理由に４社が出荷価格を一斉に改定。改定日がそろったことに対し、当時、業界内では「各社が事前に値上げで手を握っているのではないか」（関係者）と疑問視する声もあがったという。
国内ビール市場は、大手４社が９割超のシェア（占有率）を握る「寡占市場」だ。独占禁止法に詳しい伊永大輔・東北大教授によると、ビール業界はシェアが高い数社で価格が同調しやすい寡占市場として、以前は値上げ理由を公取委に報告させるなどメーカー間の一斉値上げが注視された業界の一つだったという。

title: 外国人材 都市部への転職が増加
body: 4月に外国人の在留資格「特定技能1号」の外食分野での新規受け入れが停止されてから、半年となる。【ひと目でわかる】外食分野における特定技能1号在留外国人数の推移民間調査によると、外食業では停止後に特定技能の資格を持つ国内在留の外国人の求人数が2．8倍に増加するなど、獲得競争が激化。特に地方から都市部への転職が急増しており、地方での人手不足に拍車が掛かっている。外国人材の就労支援を手掛けるマイナビグローバル（東京）によると、7月中に内定した外食業の特定技能を持つ外国人のうち、東京、神奈川、千葉、埼玉、大阪、愛知の6都府県にそれ以外の地域から転職・就職した人の割合は46．4％に上った。新規受け入れ停止前の3月は31．9％で、地方から都市部への人材移動が浮き彫りになったという。同社の杠元樹社長は調査結果について、より高い賃金を求めて都市部に転職する人は多いと分析。一方で「今の職場では特定技能2号（取得）の機会がないと思って転職する人が結構いる」とも指摘した。7月に地方のすし料理店から東京の飲食店への転職が内定したミャンマー出身の男性も取材に対し、転職理由を「料理が作りたいから」と説明した。以前は主にホールでの配膳を行っていたが、新たな職場ではキッチン業務にも携われ、月給も1万～2万円程度上がるという。「新しい仕事ではすぐに成長できると思う」と話し、2号の取得へ「もっと頑張れる」と意気込んだ。2号は家族の帯同が認められ、永住権取得への道が開ける。ただ、取得には2年間のマネジメント経験といった要件を満たす必要があり、試験では調理や接客、衛生などの飲食店運営に関わる広範な知識が問われる。このため杠氏は、地方か都市部かにかかわらず、試験に向けたサポート体制が「採用段階から非常に重要だ」と強調した。日本総合研究所の井上肇上席主任研究員は、外国人材の地方での定着には制度設計の見直しが必要だと指摘。地方で働き続ける場合には永住申請の要件を緩和したり、申請期間を短縮したりするなどの具体的なインセンティブ（優遇措置）を設けるなど「地方に残ることが合理的になる制度」の設計が重要だとの見解を示した。

title: 八田與一容疑者目撃情報 関東で増
body: 2022年に大分県別府市で発生したひき逃げ殺傷事件で、重要指名手配中の八田與一容疑者（30）に関する情報提供が、9月末までに累計で1万3978件に上っていることが分かりました。【写真を見る】八田與一容疑者の目撃情報が関東で急増　累計で約1万4000件に　特別報奨金も延長…別府ひき逃げ殺傷事件■情報提供数は累計約1万4000件　関東で急増県警に寄せられた1万3978件の情報提供のうち、八田容疑者に似た人物の目撃情報は、累計で約1万3240件に上っています。＜9月の地域別目撃情報＞（）は累計関東:73件（約4950件）近畿:28件（約1830件）九州:30件（約1680件）うち大分県内:10件（約740件）地域別の目撃情報では、関東が8月の50件から大きく増えて73件となっています。また、インターネット上の動画や画像などに関する情報は4件（累計約1230件）です。＜月別情報提供の推移＞（）は前年●2026年9月:183件（233件）8月:141件（238件）7月:382件（515件）6月:401件（706件）5月:124件（170件）4月:130件（184件）3月:138件（250件）2月:165件（165件）1月:285件（214件）●2025年12月:249件（250件）11月:278件（467件）10月:210件 （503件）9月:233件 （460件）8月:238件 （382件）7月:515件 （665件）6月:706件 （446件）殺人・殺人未遂容疑で逮捕状■9月の情報提供数は増加　報奨金延長の影響も9月の情報提供数は183件で、7月以降続いていた減少傾向から一転、8月に比べ42件増加しました。県警は、八田容疑者の重要指名手配と捜査特別報奨金の期間を2027年10月末まで延長していて、9月の情報提供件数が増加したのは、報奨金延長によって世間の関心が再度集まったことが一因ではないかとしています。県警は、指名手配容疑者の捜査強化月間となる11月に向け、新たなポスターの作成など取り組みを強化する方針です。

title: 意識回復の米死刑囚に重い症状
body: Jonathan Allen[７日 ロイター] - 米南部テネシー州で死刑執行の失敗後に意識を回復したクリスタ‌・パイク死刑囚（５０）が「怒りと混乱」の⁠状態にあり、肺炎や腕の深刻な腫れなど重い症状に苦しんでいる。弁護団が７日明らかに​した。弁護団によると、パイク死刑囚は６日に意識を取り戻し、会話が可能になった。‌州当局が自分を処刑しようとしたことを認識している一方、自身に何が起きたのか‌を尋ねたり、被害者遺‌族について質問したりしているとい​う。現在も病院のベッドに拘束された状態で、飲食や嚥下（‌えんげ）ができず、肺炎を患っている。著しく腫れた両手と‌両腕は動かせず、失わ​れた運動機能が回復するかどうかも‌不明とされる。弁護団は「長い回復への道のりになる」と⁠説明した。パイク死刑囚は１週間前、テネシー州の刑務所で薬物注射による死刑執行を受けたが、２回投与されたペント⁠バルビタールで死亡せず、意識不明​の重体となっ‌て病院に搬送された。同州では今年５月にも別の死刑囚の執行で静脈確保に失敗する事案が発生しており、⁠リー州知事は年内の死刑執行を停止して⁠調査を進めている。また州裁判所は７日、執行に使用された注射器⁠や薬剤関連資料、内部通信記録などの保存を州当局に命じ‌た。⁠弁護団は執行に使われた薬剤の成分分析などを要​求。さらにパイク死刑囚を終身刑に減刑するよう求めている。

title: 194歳ゾウガメのゲノム解析 研究
body: 世界最高齢の陸上動物とされるアルダブラゾウガメ「ジョナサン」（推定194歳）の長寿の秘密を解いた？　欧米の研究チームが老化に関わる複数の因子が他の個体と異なっていたと7日付の米科学誌サイエンス・アドバンシズに発表した。【写真で見る】陸で海で　愛くるしいカメの世界ジョナサンの体長は約110センチ。江戸時代後期の1832年生まれとされ、現在、大西洋に浮かぶ英領セントヘレナ島に生息している。アルダブラゾウガメは100歳を超える個体も珍しくないが、その記録を上回るジョナサンの健在ぶりは世界の注目を集めてきた。研究チームは長寿の秘密を探るため、ジョナサンの健康状態や島の象徴的存在であることに配慮し、血液の代わりに口腔（こうくう）内の粘膜や唾液を採取。そのゲノム（全遺伝情報）を解析し、他の4頭と比較した。その結果、傷ついたDNAを修復する遺伝子や、細胞分裂のたびに短くなる染色体末端「テロメア」を維持する仕組み、異常なたんぱく質を除去する機能、高齢になるほど増えるがんの関連遺伝子などに違いがあることが分かった。遺伝子の働きを左右する「メチル化」と呼ばれる化学変化にも特殊性が認められたという。研究チームは「長生きで知られるホッキョククジラなど他の種のデータを活用することで、がんや老化に関する理解が進むだろう」としている。【田中泰義】

title: 愛知・大村知事の発言 タイで波紋
body: 愛知・名古屋アジア大会で実施された新競技「テックボール」のタイ代表関係者が食事メニューが少なかったとSNS（交流サイト）に投稿したことに対し、愛知県の大村秀章知事が6日の定例記者会見で「来てほしくなかった」などと発言したことが、タイでも波紋を広げている。【写真で見る】3年前からピリピリムードだったアジア大会タイ紙カオソッドは6日、オンライン版で「愛知県知事が食事問題でタイの選手を『再生数稼ぎ』と非難」との趣旨の見出しで報じた。大村氏の「再生回数稼ぎに来たのかと思った」「こういう人には来てほしくなかった」との発言を紹介し、日本国内でも「発言があまりにも辛辣（しんらつ）すぎる」などの批判が出ていると解説した。他にも複数のタイメディアが、大村氏の発言を取り上げた。タイのSNSではタイ語で「偉そうで傲慢だ。こんな人にはタイにも来てほしくない」「日本人は自分たちを責める前に、いつも他人のせいにする」など、厳しい声が相次いでいる。一方、大村氏の発言やアジア大会のトラブルの影響で、日本の評判が落ちることに同情的な意見もみられた。今回のアジア大会では、タイ選手が宿泊施設に泊まれなかったり、送迎バスが遅延したりしたトラブルがタイ国内でも報じられ、大会運営を巡る問題に関心が集まっていた。一方、テックボールは、アジア・オリンピック評議会の要望を受け、組織委が運営の実務や経費を負担しないことなどを条件に正式競技に追加された経緯がある。問題となった食事について、組織委は9月、「食事は組織委が提供したものではない」と発表していた。【バンコク国本愛】

title: ガザ戦闘から3年 死者は7万4000人
body: イスラエルとイスラム組織ハマスとの戦闘が始まってから、きょうで3年となります。和平計画が停滞するなか、イスラエル軍は今もパレスチナ自治区ガザの半分以上を支配下に置き、攻撃を続けています。【写真で見る】140万人以上が深刻な食料不安…ガザの現状とは2023年10月、ハマスはイスラエル南部の住宅地や音楽イベント会場などを襲撃し、およそ1200人が死亡、250人あまりが人質として連れ去られました。これに対して、イスラエルは直後からハマス壊滅を掲げ、ガザで大規模な空爆や地上侵攻を開始。ガザ全土が激しい攻撃にさらされ、都市は壊滅的な被害を受けました。ガザ保健当局によりますと、この3年間でがれきの中から収容された人を含め7万4200人以上が死亡しました。犠牲者の多くが民間人とされ、イスラエルへの国際的な批判も強まりました。OCHA＝国連人道問題調整事務所によりますと、2026年7月から12月にかけて、人口の67%にあたる140万人以上が深刻な食料不安に直面するとされ、人道支援が不足した場合、さらに多くの住民が深刻な食料不足に陥るおそれがあります。また、ガザでは住宅の大半が損傷し、人口の9割以上が住居や生活必需品の支援を必要としているほか、学校のほとんども大規模な修繕や建て替えが必要で、多くの子どもが十分な教育を受けられない状況が続いています。こうしたなか、去年9月、アメリカのトランプ大統領は、戦闘の終結に向けた和平計画を発表。翌月にはその第1段階として停戦が発効し、ハマスが拘束していた人質とイスラエル側が拘束していたパレスチナ人の解放などが進みました。しかし、イスラエルとハマスの要求の隔たりは大きく、その後、和平計画は停滞していて、イスラエル軍は今もガザの半分以上を支配下に置いて攻撃を続けています。さらに、ガザで始まった戦火はレバノンやイランなど中東各地にも波及。地域の不安定化が続くなか、戦闘開始から3年を迎えても、ガザでの衝突を完全に終わらせる見通しは立っていません。

title: 独情報機関の元長官 スパイ容疑
body: ドイツの情報機関・BND=連邦情報局の元長官ら2人がスパイ容疑などで逮捕されました。ドイツのメディアは元長官はロシアや中国と繋がりがあったと報じています。（ロンドン　山野孝之）【動画】違法中絶 地下組織 “ジェーン”と呼ばれた女たち　かつてのメンバーと手術を受けた人を取材ドイツ連邦検察は6日、情報機関BNDのアウグスト・ハニング元長官と、部下だった元幹部をスパイ容疑などで逮捕したと発表しました。ハニング元長官は、2005年にBNDを退任した後、内務省の事務次官に就任し、退任後は、安全保障とビジネスのコンサルタントとして活動していました。検察によりますと、ハニング元長官に諜報資料を渡していたとされるBNDの元幹部は今年3月まで現職で、機密情報にアクセスできる立場にいました。元幹部からハニング元長官に提供された文書は数年間で2000件に達していました。ドイツ首相府で各省庁や各安全保障機関の幹部が出席して定期的に開催される諜報情報の共有会議のための資料など、文書の多くには機密情報が含まれていました。ドイツメディアのビルトは、ハニング元長官はロシアや中国の政府機関と繋がりがあり、ロシア大統領府とは直通ラインを持っていたと報じています。BNDはドイツの対外情報機関で、政治、経済、軍事に関する情報の収集を行っています。

title: マンジャロ求め訪日 韓国で広がり
body: 【10月07日 KOREA WAVE】韓国で、肥満症治療などを目的に「マンジャロ」の処方を受けるため日本を訪れる「スシジャロ」（「すし）」と「マンジャロ」を組み合わせた造語）が広がっている。韓国関税庁は、食品医薬品安全処の許可を受けていないマンジャロの持ち込みを摘発しており、2026年は8月までに5030件に達した。背景には日韓の価格差がある。マンジャロ2.5ミリグラムの1カ月分は韓国で30万ウォン（約3万4000円）前後だが、日本では6万〜8万ウォン（約6900〜9200円）程度と、韓国の4〜5分の1の水準だという。日本ではマンジャロが糖尿病治療薬として価格が低い水準に設定されている。円安も重なり、往復の航空運賃を考慮しても安いとの口コミが広がり、日本旅行中に購入したり、入手を目的に訪日したりする人が増えている。SNSやオンラインコミュニティーでは購入先や体験談の投稿が相次ぎ、日本の医療機関による韓国人向けの宣伝もみられる。「韓国の方歓迎」と掲げ、韓国語通訳やホテルへの配送、旅行日程に合わせた配送などをうたうほか、オンライン診療や12.5ミリグラム、15ミリグラムといった高用量、6カ月分の処方が可能と宣伝するケースもある。一方、韓国食品医薬品安全処の許可を受けていないマンジャロの持ち込みは現行法上、違法とされる。海外から持ち込まれるマンジャロは、同処が関税庁に通知した有害医薬品に指定されている。税関はエックス線検査や開封検査を実施し、輸入要件を満たさない場合は返送または廃棄している。密輸入などの法令違反が確認されれば、調査や処罰の対象となる。マンジャロなど肥満症治療薬の摘発件数は2024年の4件から2025年には1189件に急増した。安全面への懸念もある。マンジャロは原則として2〜8度での冷蔵保存が必要で、流通時には品質を維持するコールドチェーンが使われる。個人が航空機の手荷物などで運ぶ場合、適切な温度を維持できず品質が変化する恐れがあるという。江北サムスン病院家庭医学科のカン・ジェホン教授は、適切な食事や運動の指導を伴わなければ筋肉量の減少などが起きる可能性があると指摘した。運搬時の品質に加え、数カ月分を一度に処方された場合は使用期限や、医師による効果、副作用の継続的な確認にも懸念があるとしている。韓国内では、価格負担を軽減するため肥満症治療薬にも公的医療保険を適用すべきだとの意見もある。カン・ジェホン氏は保険適用の必要性を指摘する一方、保険財政への負担も考慮する必要があると述べた。（c）KOREA WAVE/AFPBB News

title: ビール大手4社カルテル疑い 調査
body: ビールの卸売業者向けの価格を調整するカルテルを結んだとして、公正取引委員会は先ほど、独占禁止法違反の疑いでメーカー大手4社に強制調査に入りました。公正取引委員会は、検察への刑事告発を視野に調査を進める方針です。【写真で見る】マンション大規模修繕でも”談合”認定　約16億円の課徴金納付命令公正取引委員会がきょう（7日）、独占禁止法違反の疑いで強制調査に入ったのは、ビールメーカー大手の▼「アサヒビール」、▼「キリンビール」、▼「サントリー」、▼「サッポロビール」の都内にある本社などです。4社は、数年前からビールの卸売業者向けの価格を調整するカルテルを結んでいた疑いがもたれています。関係者によりますと、4社は主に、加盟する業界団体「ビール酒造組合」で毎月第1木曜日に開催されていた「一木会」と呼ばれる会合にあわせて、本社の営業課長らが非公式に集まり、値上げ幅の具体的な目標を定めるなどして、カルテルを結んでいたとみられています。不適切な情報交換は長年、続いていた可能性があるということで、公正取引委員会は、押収した資料を分析するなどして、実態解明を進めるものとみられます。国税庁によりますと、ビールの2024年の市場規模は1兆1500億円。国内のビール市場は4社がシェアのほとんどを占める寡占市場で、4社は去年4月、原材料価格の高騰などを理由に主力のビール商品などを一斉値上げしています。公正取引委員会は、カルテルや入札談合などで国民生活に広く影響を及ぼし、悪質かつ重大な事案と疑われる場合に、令状に基づく捜索や証拠の差し押さえをする「犯則調査」の権限が認められています。公正取引委員会は、検察への刑事告発も視野に調査を進める方針です。【各社のコメント】▼アサヒビールアサヒビールはJNNの取材に対し、「公正取引委員会の調査を受けていることは事実」としたうえで、「調査については全面的に協力していく」とコメントしています。▼キリンビール親会社であるキリンホールディングスはHPで、調査を受けていることを認め、「当社子会社が今回の捜索を受けた事実を厳粛に受け止め、公正取引委員会の調査・要請に全面的に協力してまいります」としています。▼サントリー親会社であるサントリーホールディングスはHPで、公正取引委員会から調査を受けていることを明らかにしたうえで、「多くの方にご心配をおかけしておりますこと、深くお詫び申し上げます」「今回、立入検査を受けた事実を厳粛に受け止め、公正取引委員会の調査に対し全面的に協力してまいります」としています。▼サッポロビールサッポロビールもHPで、「本日、公正取引委員会の立入検査を受けております」「立入検査を受けた事実を真摯に受け止め、公正取引委員会の調査に全面的に協力してまいります」としています。▼ビール酒造組合「ビール酒造組合」の小野里俊哉専務理事は、JNNの取材に対し、「ビール酒造組合」も公正取引委員会の調査を受けていることを認めた上で、「内容については、調査結果が出てないので差し控えたい。調査には全面的に協力したい」と話しました。一方で、オリオンビールは、4社とともに「ビール酒造組合」を構成する会員であるものの、今回、調査対象に含まれませんでした。オリオンビールはJNNの取材に、「当社は商品の価格について自社の判断と責任において決定しており、他社との価格カルテルには関与しておりません」「今後も、関係法令を遵守するとともに関係当局から要請等があった場合には適切に対応してまいります」とコメントしました。

title: ビール大手を調査 経営層関与焦点
body:
缶ビールなどの出荷価格を巡ってカルテルを結んだ疑いが浮上し、公正取引委員会が７日、ビールメーカー大手４社に対する強制調査に乗り出した。激しい市場競争を演じてきた各社が、裏で話し合って価格を決めていた可能性が出ている。近年、価格カルテルの摘発に力を入れる公取委が今後、全容解明を図る。（小林岳人、奈良橋大輔）【グラフ】一目でわかる…ビールの店頭販売価格の推移
「まさに調査をスタートしたところだが、今回の事件の事実解明に全力投球していく」。７日の定例記者会見で、公取委の岩成博夫事務総長はそう強調した。
強制調査を受けたのは、アサヒビール、キリンビール、サントリー、サッポロビール（いずれも東京）。４社は遅くとも数年前から家庭用の缶ビールや発泡酒など、ビール類の出荷価格の値上げ幅や時期について、管理職クラスで話し合って決めていた疑いが持たれている。業界団体「ビール酒造組合」の定例会合「一木会」の後に各社幹部が集まるなどして情報交換をしていたとみられる。
ビールは、メーカーが決めた価格で卸売業者に出荷される。その後、スーパーやコンビニエンスストアなどの小売店などに流通するが、店頭での４社の主力商品は、ほぼ同価格帯で販売されることが多い。
３５０ミリ・リットル缶の店頭での想定価格は、アサヒの「スーパードライ」、キリンの「一番搾り」、サッポロの「黒ラベル」はそれぞれ２２８円前後、サントリーの「サントリー生ビール」は２１２円だ。小売り大手の関係者は「仕入れ価格も数円しか違わなく、ほとんどが横並びだ」と明かす。
２０２２年１０月と２５年４月には、原材料やエネルギー価格の高騰を理由に４社が出荷価格を一斉に改定。改定日がそろったことに対し、当時、業界内では「各社が事前に値上げで手を握っているのではないか」（関係者）と疑問視する声もあがったという。
国内ビール市場は、大手４社が９割超のシェア（占有率）を握る「寡占市場」だ。独占禁止法に詳しい伊永大輔・東北大教授によると、ビール業界はシェアが高い数社で価格が同調しやすい寡占市場として、以前は値上げ理由を公取委に報告させるなどメーカー間の一斉値上げが注視された業界の一つだったという。

title: 公取委 なぜビール4社に強制調査
body: スーパーや飲食店で販売されるビールの価格でカルテルを結んだ疑いがあるとして、公正取引委員会が7日、独占禁止法違反（不当な取引制限）の疑いで、大手ビールメーカー4社を家宅捜索した。【図解】銀座に集うビール大手幹部の非公式会議　公取委の30年越しの追跡刑事事件化を視野に入れた強制調査は約1年ぶり。公取委は、行政処分を前提とした立ち入り検査をするのが一般的だが、なぜ強制調査に踏み切ったのか。関係者によると、公取委が捜索に入ったのは、いずれも東京都に本社があるアサヒビール（墨田区）、キリンビール（中野区）、サントリー（港区）、サッポロビール（渋谷区）。4社は、メーカーから卸売業者に出荷する「生産者価格」について、1リットル当たりの値上げ幅に合意し、価格を調整した疑いがあるという。家宅捜索は、刑事告発を前提とした「犯則調査権」に基づく。国税庁や証券取引等監視委員会にも与えられている権限で、裁判所に令状請求し、強制的に捜索や証拠の差し押さえができる。公取委がこの権限を使うのは、軽油販売をめぐるカルテル事件で調査に入った2025年9月以来。過去には、東京五輪をめぐる談合事件や、リニア中央新幹線建設工事をめぐる談合事件などの例もある。公取委は、自由な経済活動を妨げる企業の違反行為に目を光らせるのが役割だ。違反の疑いがあれば、通例は、立ち入り検査などの行政調査をする。違反企業には、課徴金納付命令や、再発防止を求める排除措置命令などの行政処分をする。これに対し、犯則調査は検察庁への告発が前提だ。告発を受けた検察は起訴すべきかどうかを判断する。このため、最終的に法人や個人の刑事責任が問われるケースが多い。公取委は犯則調査の条件として、国民生活に大きな影響を与えると考えられる悪質かつ重大な事案と、違反を繰り返すなど行政処分では公正な競争環境が回復できない疑いのある事案を挙げている。国税庁によると、ビールの小売店と飲食店での消費量は233万キロリットルで、アルコール飲料全体の3割を占める。消費者に身近な商品で、4社は市場で高いシェアを持つ。こうした事情を重くみて、強制調査に踏み切った模様だ。（長妻昭明）

title: TOPIX構成銘柄 1634→986社へ
body: 日本取引所グループ（JPX）は7日、日本の代表的な株価指数である東証株価指数（TOPIX）の構成銘柄を、大幅に入れ替えると発表した。銘柄数は現行の1634社から986社となる。東京証券取引所の市場再編の一環で、10月末から2028年7月まで段階的に実施する。27年10月に再評価があり、実際の銘柄数は変動しうる。28年10月以降は毎年定期的に銘柄を入れ替える。【図表】市場の評価低い銘柄は「退場」へ　採用企業に緊張感株価指数は、さまざまな企業の株が取引される株式市場全体やある銘柄群の値動きを、一定の計算法に基づき一目で分かるようにしたもの。TOPIXの他、日経平均株価や米国のダウ工業株平均、S＆P500なども有名だ。TOPIXは1969年に旧東証1部上場企業すべての値動きを反映する指数としてつくられた。対象銘柄の時価総額（株価×株式数）をもとに算出され、68年を100とし、上昇や下落はポイントで表す。

title: トラブル相次ぐ歯の自由診療 なぜ
body:
自由診療のインプラントや歯列矯正をめぐるトラブルが後を絶たない。新規参入する歯科医院が増え、「格安」「無料」を謳ったSNS広告や価格競争の激化も背景に、患者が十分な情報を得られないまま高額治療の契約をするケースも指摘されている。安心して治療に臨むためにはどうしたらよいのか。歯科業界の課題とともに検証する。（取材・文：川口穣／Yahoo!ニュース オリジナル 特集編集部）
岐阜県在住の宮川淳子さん（仮名）は2024年8月、自宅から遠く離れた西日本エリアの歯科医院で、「オールオン4（フォー）インプラント」と呼ばれる治療を受けた。残っていた歯をすべて抜き、チタン製の杭を上下4本ずつ埋め込んで仮歯を載せる大手術。特に上あごは、長い土台を頬骨にまで打ち込む「ザイゴマインプラント」という手法だった。その日以降、彼女が「地獄」と表現する日々が続くことになる。「手術の後は腫れと痛みで目も開けられず、口中血だらけで、タクシーには乗車拒否されながらなんとかホテルに帰り着きました。何日経ってもズキズキずっと痛くて固形物は噛めないし、夜も眠れない日が続きました」
インプラントは例外的なケースを除いて「自由診療」（自費診療）で、各医療機関が個別に費用を設定し、患者側が原則として全額を負担する。保険診療より患者負担が高額になりやすく、契約内容やリスクの認識違いなどからトラブルが起こることもある。
手術から2カ月後、仮歯を人工歯に入れ替える処置を受けたが、上下の歯がかみ合わない。痛みも引かなかった。約4カ月間、痛みに耐えて診察に通ったが、ただ「大丈夫、順調です」と言われるだけ。歯科医師が現れず、歯科衛生士による診察だけのこともあったという。2025年春になり、顔面麻痺を発症したことで宮川さんはこの医院へ通うことを諦めた。「このままだと殺されると思った。別の病院へ行くとひどい状態だと言われました。『設備の整った病院でやり直すしかない』って」

title: Spanish pensioner whose eviction sparked nationwide protests dies, union says
summary: Maricarmen Abascal, 87, was forcibly removed on a stretcher from her apartment of more than 70 years in September.
body:
Maricarmen Abascal was evicted from her flat in Madrid two weeks ago
An elderly woman whose eviction sparked nationwide protests over Spain's housing crisis and a political row that triggered early elections has died, according to Madrid's tenants union.
Maricarmen Abascal, 87, was forcibly removed on a stretcher from her apartment of more than 70 years on 23 September after she was unable to afford rent increases.
The company that owned the flat later offered to allow her to return at a lower rate - but she was unable to sign an agreement as she had been admitted to hospital.
"We regret to announce that Maricarmen passed away today," the Madrid Tenants' Union said in a statement, adding her situation marked "a turning point in the history of this country".
Union spokesperson Alicia del Río said: "Speculation costs lives, and today rentierism has finished killing our colleague Maricarmen" but "her memory lives on with us".
A cause of death was not announced.
Abascal's death was received in Puerta del Sol with a big collective gasp, then followed by a minute of silence.
It is in this square in the centre of Madrid where thousands have been camping since Abascal's eviction last month to demand more affordable housing.
On Wednesday, it became the place to pay tribute to her.
People lit dozens of candles around the square in a small improvised vigil that glowed with a warm light on a dry and warm autumn night.
Other candles formed an altar to Abascal in front of the headquarters of the Community of Madrid government.
Messages on cardboard banners next to the candles read "it's not a death, it's a killing", "the fight will continue" and "Mari Carmen, the grandmother of the whole country", among others.
A few hundred people then took to the streets that connect Puerta del Sol with the Spanish Congress, just 500m away, in an improvised protest.
During the march people chanted: "We will not tolerate a single eviction more" and "the fight will continue, Mari Carmen is still alive". There were other chants against fascism and against the police.
The police had set up barriers to block the march. There was not a big police presence, and there was the tension that protests sometimes have.
Many protesters seemed to feel the police have been complicit in the evictions, as under court orders they have to remove tenants who have been served eviction notices.
After a couple of hours, the chants near Congress gave way to another minute of silence. Then, a big collective shout of "murderers".
Wednesday night's march has finished, but the camping, already on its 12th night, will continue "as long as necessary" one of the protesters told the BBC.
Abascal became a symbol for Spain's housing crisis following her eviction.
Her father first rented the property in 1956 and she continued as the tenant after her parents died, during which time there was a cap on the rent.
However, Urbagestión, which bought the property in 2018, increased the rent from €500 per month (£428; $572) to €2,650 (£2,280; $3,020).
The company later offered to reduce this to €1,650 - still €300 more than Abascal's monthly pension.
Three previous attempts to evict her were blocked by the courts and the case has received increasing media attention.
Anger over the situation grew, leading to protests and putting pressure on the coalition government to approve emergency housing legislation -but it was rejected in Congress last week.
That led to further protests,with tens of thousands of people takingto the streetsin cities across the country over the weekend.
Protesters gathered at one of Madrid's main squares, Puerta del Sol, following Absacal's death
Referring to the rejected bills, the Madrid Tenants' Union said: "While a historic agreement was reached that would have allowed her to return to her home, this solution has come too late. An absolutely avoidable situation after a torturing process."
It said the events surrounding her eviction represented a turning point in the country's history, but added that the cost to get to this point had been "too high".
"Above all, we will fulfil what she always asked of us: 'fight, keep fighting for what is yours'," it said.
In a video recorded from her hospital bed following her eviction, Maricarmen said: "I haven't managed to defend my home, but I have fought so that others can learn to fight for what's theirs."
"All my love goes to Maricarmen's family and loved ones," Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said. "A hug as well to everyone who today feels this loss as their own."
Opposition People's Party leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo also sent his condolences to Maricarmen's loved ones, as he said on X: "No campaign, no parties, no self-interested exploitation. No more stones in the wall.
"In the face of a person's death, only respect is in order," he added.
Earlier on Wednesday, unions had called a general strike to take place on 11 November, demanding housing reforms.
The public outcry over Abascal's situation has led to political turmoil in Spain.
On Monday Sánchez, who leads a leftist coalition that does not hold a majority in parliament, called an early election for 29 November. It followed his failure to get the emergency housing legislation through Congress.
The political right had argued that the government's attempt to intervene in the housing market would have led to fewer homes being rented and would have raised prices further.
Speaking on Monday, Sánchez said he needed "a broader progressive majority" that can "overcome the resistance of the elites" to push through reforms.
Other issues not relating to housing, such as numerous corruption scandals linked to his party, and pressures relating to the cost of living and immigration, have also caused him problems.
Most opinion polls suggest the conservatives are likely to emerge as the largest party in the next election. However, they would be expected to need the support of the hard-right Vox party to form a government.
Additional reporting by Tom McArthur

title: Israelis mourn 7 October attack victims three years after deadly Hamas raid
summary: Memorial events have taken place in Israel on the third anniversary of the Hamas-led attack that sparked the devastating Gaza war.
body:
A man comforts a woman at the fountain at Dizengoff Square on Wednesday
Memorial events have taken place in Israel on the third anniversary of the devastating Hamas-led attack there that sparked the war in Gaza.
Families paid tribute to their loved ones at some of the sites where about 1,200 people were killed in the assault and 251 were taken hostage.
"The nation unites on this day in the longing for our dear ones," said Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who faced calls from protesters for an independent state inquiry into security failures that day.
In response to the attack, Israel launched a military offensive in Gaza which has killed more than 74,200 people, according to the Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are seen as reliable by the UN.
Residents of kibbutz destroyed in 7 October Hamas-led attacks grapple with how to rebuild
Violence has continued in Gazadespite a ceasefire agreedalmost a year ago and living conditions for the 2.1 million people living there remain dire.
On Wednesday morning, bereaved families and survivors gathered at a memorial for the 378 people who were killed at the Nova dance festival in southern Israel on 7 October 2023.
The festival site was near Kibbutz Re'im and not far from the border with Gaza, from where Hamas-led gunmen launched their dawn attack.
Witnesses have described how festival-goers were shot, sexually abused and tortured by gunmen during the raid.
Forty-four people were kidnapped, of whom 25 were brought back from Gaza alive.
Ahuva Yavin Mayze, whose21-year-old daughter Adiwas shot and killed at Nova, told the BBC what happened at the sitewas "dystopic, unimaginable".
At the Nova festival, 378 people were killed, with 44 more taken hostage
"Today is a difficult day, not only for me but for a large part of the nation," said Shlomo Sharf, a former Israeli footballer, in comments reported by Channel 12.
He paid tribute to his granddaughter, May Naim, 24, who was also killed at the festival.
Former hostage Yarden Bibas, whose wife and two young sons were kidnapped from their home in Kibbutz Nir Oz and later killedin captivity in Gaza, was quoted by the Times of Israel as saying: "Shiri, Ariel and Kfir. Sorry. Sorry that you are up there and I am here."
Residents and relatives pay tribute beside graves in Kfar Aza, Israel
Crowds also filed into the small cemetery at Kibbutz Kfar Aza, where 64 residents were killed and 19 were taken hostage on 7 October.
Zion Regev, a community leader, said most surviving residents had yet to return to their homes because of the trauma of what happened.
"This is the first time we are doing all the things here in the kibbutz," he told Reuters news agency. "It's a very emotional day, it's a very difficult day for our community, three years after 7 October."
A man who reportedly helped to fend off Hamas attackers at Kibbutz Magen praised IDF troops who "fought so bravely" during the raid.
Speaking to crowds at the national memorial event at Tel Aviv's Yarkon Park on Wednesday evening, Ido Yakir said Israel would remember everyone "who knew that they had to give their lives in order to save others".
In a statement released by his office on Wednesday afternoon, Netanyahu said he had lit a memorial candle commemorating every victim of 7 October.
"We will complete the mission: we have settled the score and will continue settling the score with all the murderers," he added.
At a ceremony on Monday marking the Jewish calendar's anniversary of the attack, the prime minister said Israel had killed 4,000 out of the 6,000 Palestinians who infiltrated Israel from Gaza that day.
The water of the fountain at Dizengoff Square in Tel Aviv was stained red to symbolise blood
In Tel Aviv's Dizengoff Square, Israeli anti-government protesters dyed the fountain red to mark the anniversary of the attack.
The fountain has been used as a memorial site for those killed, with pictures, flowers and messages laid around the basin wall.
Protesters also briefly blocked one of the main highways in the city to hold a moment of silence on Wednesday morning.
They held banners that read, "the people will remember their sons and daughters", along with others that said "a complete failure" and "guilty" next to an image of Netanyahu.
Many senior Israeli defence and security officials have resigned or been fired since the attack took place. But there has not been an independent commission of inquiry into Israel's worst security failure.
The prime minister has rejected any personal responsibility and has refused to establish a state inquiry led by Israel's Supreme Court, arguing recently that the country's judiciary would be biased against him.
Einav Zangauker became an outspoken critic of the Netanyahu government while her son, Matan, was in captivity in Gaza. He was released last October as part of the ceasefire agreement.
"They're trying to make us forget what happened on 7 October," she told Army Radio. "We won't forget, we will demand the truth."
Dalit Ram Aharon and her husband Achi say they want to move back to Nir Oz "in the memory" of the friends they lost
Memorial events were organised in other countries around the world, including in Germany, where the Jewish students' union held a vigil at Berlin's Brandenburg Gate.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said the Hamas-led attack marked a "profound rupture".
"We commemorate the victims, we share their pain," he said, adding that antisemitism must be confronted with "even greater resolve".
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham told Britain's Jewish community: "We stand with you."
"The impact of the attacks has been felt not just in Israel, but in Jewish communities across the world who still bear the burden of the tragic events that day," he said.
Outside Downing Street, a vigil was also held to commemorate British-Israelis killed in the initial attack, later as hostages, or in fighting with Hamas.
Ursula von der Leyen, the president of the European Commission, said: "The unspeakable savagery and terror of 7 October must never happen again."
She also said that the European Union "remains ready to help turn today's fragile ceasefire into a durable peace, based on a two-state solution."
Speaking to reporters outside the White House on Wednesday, US President Donald Trump said he had spoken to Netanyahu and wished the people of Israel well.
"That was a horrible day, a horrible tragedy," he said.
Families in Gaza are increasingly worried about where they will end up
This is the first anniversary of the 7 October attack with no hostages remaining in Gaza, but a US-brokered ceasefire deal from last year has failed to deliver peace or bring security.
There has been no end to Gaza's deadliest ever war, as Israel continues to carry out near-daily attacks.
More than 1,460 people have been killed there since the ceasefire took effect, according to Gaza health ministry. The Israeli military says at least seven Israeli soldiers have been killed in the strip over the same period.
Most of Gaza is in ruins, with nearly all the 2.1 million population still displaced amid dire humanitarian conditions.
An estimated 80% of all structures have been destroyed or damaged during the war, leaving more than 60 million tonnes of rubble piled up and 1.2 million people living in tents or shelters, according to the UN.
Families who have been displaced several times during the war increasingly ask where they could go next, and whether they might even be forced to leave Gaza altogether.
Mohammed Emad al-Din, a 38-year-old father of two who works as a barber in Gaza City, said he had been displaced five times. His home was destroyed and his barber shop was partially damaged.
He told the BBCthat the fear of being forced out of Gaza now follows him even into his dreams.
"I don't believe Israel caused all this destruction for nothing," he said.
"They have turned Gaza into a place that is almost impossible to live in, and I fear that we will eventually end up outside the place where we were born."
Another displaced Palestinian, Atta Saeed Hassan Shweikh, told the BBC that his son, daughter, sister and her children had all been killed during the war.
Speaking from Gaza City, he said Palestinians were "living in graves while still alive" and have endured "severe suffering".
At least three Palestinians were killed in Israeli strikes in the northern town of Beit Lahia and the southern city of Khan Younis on Wednesday, medics said.
The Israeli military said it struck two Hamas operatives in northern Gaza overnight, one of whom it accused of planting explosives near the so-called Yellow Line, which marks the territory still occupied by Israeli forces.
Hamas-which is proscribed as a terrorist organisation by Israel, the UK and others-released a statement  praising the 7 October attack as a "historic milestone" in its "ongoing struggle project".
The statement, attributed to the group and disseminated in Palestinian media, called the attack "a natural response" to "bitter suffering" imposed by Israel.

title: Israelis demand accountability over 7 October failures three years after attacks
summary: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has refused to take any personal responsibility for what happened or order a state inquiry.
body:
Residents of Kfar Aza attended a memorial ceremony on Wednesday for those killed on 7 October 2023
As the sky began to lighten over Israel's border with Gaza on Wednesday, the people of Kfar Aza moved silently towards the armoury at the centre of the kibbutz.
It was there, shortly after 07:00 on 7 October 2023, that Hamas-led attackers killed half the community's 14-member civil defence squad. They were among 64 killed and 19 kidnapped from the community that day.
The pain of those attacks is still fresh here. But three years on, there are questions about who else should pay the price for Israel's security failure.
"I need my country to take responsibility," said Inbar Goldstein, whose brother and niece were killed, and four other relatives kidnapped from Kfar Aza.
The 7 October attack was the deadliest Israel had suffered since its creation in 1948. About 1,200 people were killed across southern Israel by gunmen who broke through the border fence and attacked communities there. Another 251 people were taken back to Gaza as hostages.
Three years on from Israel's biggest security failure, there is still no independent state inquiry into how it was allowed to happen.
And the man in charge at the time of that failure - Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu - is running for election again, with the same campaign promise: to be stronger and tougher than anyone else in protecting Israel from its enemies.
"Nobody investigated the roots [of the attack]. It didn't start or end on October 7th - it's a long process of abandonment," Goldstein said.
More than 60 residents of Kfar Aza were killed by Hamas-led gunmen and 19 were taken hostage three years ago
Aside from Hamas's responsibility for the attack itself, there are growing questions in Israel around what caused the country's intelligence failure, what information was passed to military and political leaders in the run-up to the attacks, and what Netanyahu himself knew.
For months beforehand, young female soldiers posted at bases along the Gaza border to watch for suspicious activity had warned their superiors about possible preparations for an attack.
Among them was Roni Eshel. She was killed with 14 other members of her unit when gunmen overran their base at Nahal Oz, just next to Kfar Aza.
"There are so many questions," her uncle Elad Levy told me. "Were the Egyptians warning the prime minister? The Emiratis? Were there no other warnings Netanyahu ignored?  We need to find out what happened – not just on the day, but the year before, and five years before that."
"The truth should be clear," he continued. "If we don't inquire into this, it will happen again and again."
They were Israel's 'eyes on the border' - their warnings went unheard
Benjamin Netanyahu has rejected any personal responsibility for security failures three years ago
Over the past three years, there have been mounting reports of warnings being given to Netanyahu - by his own security chief, as well as by regional neighbours – which he denies.
Last month, Israel's Haaretz newspaper published extracts from a new book, alleging that the leader of the United Arab Emirates had called Netanyahu 10 days before the attack to warn of Hamas plans for a major operation.
Netanyahu's office has dismissed the report as "an absolute lie" and has said he will sue the newspaper.
Amir Ohana, a member of Netanyahu's Likud party, said in a social media video last month that it was "preposterous and absurd" to suggest that Netanyahu could have known about the attack when the former Hamas leader in Gaza, Yahya Sinwar, had only told a handful of people.
Israel's prime minister, he said, had since reshaped the Middle East and did not give up, "even when voices inside and outside Israel called on him to stop".
Netanyahu has blamed his own security chiefs for the failures that led to the 7 October attacks, accusing them of deliberately choosing not to wake him in the hours beforehand, for fear that he would order a massive deployment of the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) and escalate the situation.
"God forbid we wake up the prime minister and he says, 'Wake up the entire IDF immediately, scramble the air force!'" he told Israel's right-wing Channel 14 television network.
"What would have happened if they had woken me? This would not have happened," he said, suggesting that his response would have better protected Israel from the attacks.
Netanyahu denied reports that he was warned by the UAE's president days before Hamas attacked
Yaakov Katz, a journalist and author of several books on Israel's defence, has written about the growing concerns over Hamas activity that emerged in the hours leading up to the assault.
In his book, While Israel Slept, he describes calls between senior military figures and intelligence chiefs in the early hours of the morning, the sudden recall of commanders from leave, and the dispatch of an elite intelligence unit to the border.
He told me their expectation was, at worst, a small, limited incursion by Hamas fighters.
"So why would [Netanyahu] order a massive pre-emptive strike by the IDF, if every security chief is telling him this is not what this is going to be? Waking him would not have made a difference."
But he said Netanyahu faced other questions about his failure to spot what was happening.
"You were the prime minister, you set the policy," he said. "You created a doctrine and a policy of containment that trickled down to the last soldier manning the watchtower on the border with Gaza: contain Hamas, separate the Palestinians, and keep Hamas in power to prevent the establishment of a Palestinian state."
Israelis have held protests to demand the establishment of a state commission of inquiry
For years, Netanyahu oversaw a policy of containing - not confronting - Hamas in Gaza, during which Israeli governments allowed Qatar to provide hundreds of millions of dollars of aid for Gaza.
A month after the 7 October attacks, he told a German newspaper that claims he wanted to strengthen Hamas were "an absolute lie".
"On the contrary we wanted to continue to weaken Hamas as much as we could," he told Die Welt. "But the money was meant to avoid a civilian catastrophe - that is the only reason."
Months after the attack, the IDF's then-chief of staff, Lt Gen Herzi Halevi, publicly apologised for the failure to defend civilians, saying he carried that weight on his shoulders and in his heart.
He resigned. A raft of military commanders were later fired, and Israel's domestic intelligence chief left his position.
Netanyahu has so far rejected any personal responsibility for the attacks.
Col Richard Hecht was the IDF's international spokesman on 7 October. He told me the refusal of political leaders - including Netanyahu - to accept responsibility was part of the reason he resigned six months later.
"It's a disgrace," he told me. "When you look at accountability, within the IDF I don't think there's a problem. And that's the pain. That's one of the main causes of bad blood between the political echelon and the military."
At a memorial ceremony in Jerusalem on Monday, the father of one of those killed on 7 October stood up to challenge the prime minister.
"You didn't protect my son, you didn't protect all those who were murdered," he said, before security guards led him away. "Shame! Disgrace!"
"Netanyahu does not surrender" is a slogan of his right-wing Likud party
Three years on from the attacks, calls for accountability are growing. Campaigners have asked Israel's highest court to force the government into establishing a state commission of inquiry.
Yizhar Shai, a former minister and opposition politician whose youngest son Yaron, a soldier, was killed on 7 October, is part of that campaign.
"We are going into these elections almost blindfolded as it relates to October 7th," he told me during a protest in Tel Aviv last week. "Our prime minister has never given a detailed, thorough explanation under oath, where he would be asked all the tough questions and have to explain everything."
Netanyahu has consistently refused a state inquiry led by Israel's Supreme Court, arguing recently that the country's judiciary would be biased against him.
Before calling an election, his government proposed an alternative "national commission of inquiry", whose members would be appointed by political parties.
But despite passing a raft of other legislation before parliament ended its session in July, Israel's government said it ran out of time to pass a bill setting out its plans for the inquiry.
We approached several members of his Likud party for an interview, without success. We also requested that the party respond to their critics, and are waiting for their response.
Gadi Eisenkot and other opposition leaders have backed calls for a state commission of inquiry
Netanyahu's denial of responsibility has now become an election issue, as he prepares to run for re-election later this month.
A video game called Sleepy Bibi, released by the team of his main opponent, Gadi Eisenkot, asks players to help the prime minister avoid responsibility by dodging warnings of an attack and "making it to bed safely".
Netanyahu has styled himself for decades as Israel's "Mr Security", and despite presiding over the worst security failure in Israel's history, is running on the same security platform again.
For the past three years, he focused on waging new wars against Israel's enemies - Hamas, Hezbollah and Iran.
Polls suggest a close race, and that the 7 October attacks are central to many voters' decisions.
Yaakov Katz says the legacy of 7 October is a coin with two sides.
"There are the failures, the mistakes that led to the Hamas invasion," he told me. "But there's the other side, which is Netanyahu's argument; that [he] has re-engineered the Middle East and made Israel a safer place today. And that is an argument Israelis take with them to the polls."

title: France halts use of stun grenades after boy's hand blown off in student protests
summary: The step comes after several groups complained of police using disproportionate force towards teenagers.
body:
Hundreds of thousands of protesters took to the streets across France on Tuesday, including in the capital Paris
France has suspended the use of stun grenades for policing student protests that have swept the country, after a 15-year-old's hand was blown off earlier this week.
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said he had requested the pause until the facts of Monday's incident in Lens had been "clarified", with conflicting accounts offered by protesters and officials.
The disruption continued on Wednesday with more than 500 schools fully or partially shut.
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has defended the police response, afterseveral groups complained of police using disproportionate force towards teenagers.
In an address to the nation on Wednesday evening, he denied security forces had "orders to confront" the young people.
He said the government would look into the demands made by students and promised they would present a set of proposals at the end of October, ranging from renovating buildings to make more teachers available. He gave no further details.
The "anger of young people does not come from nowhere," he said.
Education Minister Édouard Geffray said 24 schools had been "set alight or vandalised" to such an extent that they would be shut for several weeks, affecting 30,000 pupils.
Hundreds of thousands of people took to the streets on Tuesday to call for better school conditions and in some cities tear gas and water cannon were deployed. The interior ministry said 488 people were arrested and 43 members of the security forces were hurt.
Nuñez told French radio RTL that police watchdog IGPN had opened 18 investigations to determine whether officers had been "proportionate" during the demonstrations, which have spread from high school pupils to their parents, university students and unions.
Watch: Why has the use of stun grenades been suspended during the student protests?
"There is a police action that raises questions for all of us within the Ministry of the Interior; it's what happened in Lens," he said as he confirmed the suspension of stun grenades -weapons which are considered non-lethal and send out small rubber pellets when they detonate.
The 15-year-old boy's hand was torn off after aso-called anti-encirclement grenade was fired in unclear circumstancesnear the Auguste Béhal high school in the northern city near Lille.
Authorities have said he picked up the grenade which then exploded, but students have alleged he was hit directly after an officer fired. According to the local prefect, police had been confronted by more than 200 students throwing stones and fireworks.
The national secretary of policing union UNSA said he was sceptical about the move, saying it had been based "on emotion".
"We are dealing with increasingly violent people," Jean-Paul Nascimento told FranceInfo, cautioning that without the weapon to disperse crowds there may be more clashes at close quarters. "That's where there will perhaps be even more injuries," he warned.
Protests were largely peaceful on Wednesday, but tensions flared near Paris's Sciences Po university as officers used tear gas and pushed protesters back along a barricaded street
Concerns have also been stoked by the case of a 14-year-old hit in the face with a tear gas grenade last week. The boy's lawyer said he had lost several teeth and suffered a fractured jaw in the incident at Saint-Ouen-l'Aumône, north-west of Paris, and a police officer has been charged.
And in a separate development on Wednesday, a 16-year-old suffered a serious hand injury outside a school in Strasbourg, reportedly while handling a mortar firework.
Prosecutors also said an investigation for attempted murder had been opened after a 17-year-old student protester complained an officer "held his head underwater" while trying to arrest him near a river in the north-eastern city of Belfort. French reports say the boy has himself been charged with aggravated assault for allegedly attacking the officer.
Addressing France's National Assembly on Wednesday, both Nuñez and Education Minister Geffray said the speed at which the protests had turned violent was unprecedented.
Tear gas in Paris and Marseille as school protests grow across France
School protests send shivers down French government's spine
Geffray said dozens of headteachers and deputies had been injured, many deliberately so, and alleged the movement had been "very quickly infiltrated by ultra-violent groups".
"We have never seen anything like this," he said of the disorder which officials report has harmed more than 200 students and 700 police officers, and prompted more than 6,600 arrests.
Nuñez later said he found it "excessive to speak of police repression of the movement", insisting that officers were only acting in response to violence and damage.
The national coordinator of the radical-left France Unbowed (LFI) party said that it had taken "several children being maimed for life for Nuñez to give up using grenades against high school students".
The prime minister has accused LFI of trying to "sow chaos" during the protests ahead of elections to select President Emmanuel Macron's successor in April.
Its leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon is currently second in the opinion polls behind Marine Le Pen of the hard-right National Rally - who on Wednesday said Macron was "always on the side of attacking the police".
The president held an emergency meeting late on Tuesday with Prime Minister Lecornu and other key ministers to find a way out of the crisis after almost a quarter of alllycéeswere disrupted by the day's protests - with government figures putting the number of protesters at more than 250,000.
Lecornu announced that schools should set aside half the day for students to voice their concerns, and noted on social media that an online consultation seeking their opinions had drawn 30,000 responses within a day.
But students' unions - who put the number of protesters at 450,000 - maintain a fourth round of demonstrations is planned for Thursday in Paris and other cities, and told reporters they had requested a meeting with Lecornu due to a lack of "concrete measures" outlined so far.
The union representing school leaders told FranceInfo that a solution would require "something more than simple consultation periods", while the head of the USL high school union, Ryad Rani, told French radio on Wednesday: "We are telling M. Nuñez, calm your police officers down and call for restraint."

title: Canada suspends plans to expand assisted dying to people with mental illness
summary: People with mental illness alone were to be eligible for assisted dying in Canada in March 2027, but that has now been paused indefinitely.
body:
Minister of Justice Sean Fraser also announced plans to allow for advanced consent to the programme
Canada says it will indefinitely suspend plans to expand its medically assisted dying law to people whose sole condition is mental illness, citing a lack of consensus on who would be eligible.
It comes after a parliamentary panel earlier this year recommended that medically assisted dying - known as Maid in Canada - should not be expanded.
On Wednesday, Canada's justice minister, Sean Fraser, said that "while there is not a perfect consensus on this issue, we believe this is the correct approach at this particular time".
Supporters of extending the programme to those with mental illness alone argue that not doing so violates their constitutional rights and access to medical care.
A federal case remains before the courts challenging the government's earlier decision to delay access to Maid for people with mental illness.
Fraser acknowledged this is an issue that the Supreme Court could weigh on in the future.
Wednesday's announcement means that Canadians with mental illness as their sole condition will not be able to access assisted dying by March 2027 as previously planned.
The government will instead introduce a new law in the coming weeks that suspends that expansion indefinitely, Fraser said.
That proposed legislation will also to allow patients who have a progressing incurable illness to consent to assisted dying before their health deteriorates to the point where they are unable to do so.
However, it will leave the final decision up to individual provinces.
Advanced requests are not currently legal under federal law, but are allowed in Quebec for those with serious and incurable illnesses.
"These are not easy decisions but we believe they will be the correct ones," Fraser said.
Medically assisted dying became legal in Canada in 2016 for people with terminal illnesses, who still account for the vast majority of cases.
Following a court case in Quebec, it was expanded in 2021 to people with incurable conditions but whose death was not imminent.
Canada was first set to expand its assisted dying laws to people whose sole condition is mental illness in 2023, but it delayed doing so twice to allow for time to study its potential delivery.
Advocates for expanding assisted dying to people with mental illness alone say they should have the same rights as patients with other types of illness.
In a statement, advocacy group Dying with Dignity called the government's decision  "profoundly disappointing".
"We anticipate that a very small number of individuals with severe and persistent mental illness would be eligible for Maid under this criterion, but their suffering is no less real than those who live with physical illnesses," said Helen Long, the group's CEO.
But concerns have been raised about whether mental illnesses are currently understood well enough by medicine to determine appropriate eligibility.
"When I hear that there is a lack of consensus in the medical community about the irremediable nature of certain mental illnesses, that gives me real cause for concern," Fraser said.
Canada should 'indefinitely exclude' people with mental illness from assisted dying, report says
What is a 'safe death'? Mentally ill woman asks for assisted dying in Canada
'I could live 30 years but plan to die': How assisted dying law is dividing Canadians
Claire Brosseau, a woman with treatment resistant bipolar 1 disorder who is part of the federal case challenging Canada's current laws, told the BBC earlier this year that assisted dying would offer her "a safe death".
Brosseau's lawyer, Michael Fenrick, told the BBC on Wednesday that he anticipates a lengthy legal battle on the issue.
"People will continue to suffer intolerably while the case goes through the courts," he said.
More broadly, some experts have also raised concerns that Canada's assisted dying programme has become a tool to alleviate the suffering of people who would be better served by improved access to affordable housing and healthcare, and not an option of last resort.
In a report earlier this year, a parliamentary committee noted competing opinions on the issue but recommended Canada "indefinitely exclude persons whose sole underlying medical condition is a mental illness" from assisted dying.
It added that there is a "pressing need for increased and more equitable access to adequate mental health services".
The conclusions were made after committee members heard from doctors, advocates and experts from countries that do allow assisted dying for people solely with mental illness, like the Netherlands and Belgium.
Not all committee members agreed with its recommendation, and some released a dissenting report arguing the process was "fundamentally flawed" and "biased".
Polls suggestthe majority of Canadians support access,externalto medically assisted death but that support falls when it comes to patients with mental illness alone.
Watch: One mentally ill man's fight for assisted dying in Canada
If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support can be found atthe BBC's Action Line.
In Canada, support can be found at the Suicide Crisis Helpline by dialling 988

title: 'Stop throwing shade' - the woman trying to stop firms leaving the UK
summary: British people need more incentives to invest in big firms listed in the UK, Dame Julia Hoggett, boss of the London Stock Exchange, says.
body:
Dame Julia Hoggett says negative sentiment about the UK market has pushed companies to leave in the past
The UK needs to do more back its own companies at a time when a growing number are choosing to list their shares in the US rather than at home, the boss of the London Stock Exchange (LSE) has told the BBC.
Dame Julia Hoggett said the government needed to make it "more attractive" to invest in the UK stock market, otherwise big firms would continue to look overseas for their next stage of growth.
Over the last few years,scores of big firms have left the London market, are considering a move or have been bought by private foreign investors.
The fear is this weakens the UK economy by reducing tax revenues and depressing business valuations.
"If we want Britain to back Britain, which is what I hear the chancellor and the prime minister saying, then let's make sure that we're creating structural incentives to do so," Dame Julia told the BBC'sBig Boss podcast.
"We need to take the handbrake off."
The LSE's main market is made up of around 930 companies with a total market value of about £4.9 trillion.
Almost 40% are international businesses, hailing from over 80 countries.
But in the last few years, many firms have delisted or moved away from the LSE, including takeaway chain Just Eat, which joined the Amsterdam stock exchange,  travel giant Tui which opted for Frankfurt, and Paddy Power-owner Flutter which now trades in New York.
Meanwhile, the number of companies newly listing their shares in London has dwindled.
Last year, there were 23 initial public offerings (IPOs) on the London market, with £2.1bn raised. In the US, which has much larger capital markets, there were 354 with $44bn (£33bn) raised.
It has coincided in a big rise of UK investment money flowing into US stocks in search of better returns.
"We talk as a nation about wanting growth in every postcode, but at the moment, a lot of us are funding growth in every zip code," Dame Julia said.
There was "no shortage of great companies and no shortage of capital", she added.
But negative sentiment about the UK market - which was often exaggerated - had contributed to companies leaving in the past, she said.
"We need to stop throwing shade at ourselves as a nation... it's a national habit."
Big Boss Interview: LSE's Dame Julia Hoggett
The boss of the London Stock Exchange speaks to the BBC about the attraction of the UK as a place for companies to list.
However, she said British people needed more "incentives" to invest in UK stocks.
She wants the government to scrapthe 0.5% tax,externalBritons pay when they purchase UK shares, pointing out there is no tax when they buy foreign stocks.
She also supports the idea of tax credits for Britons investing domestically. The UK had such a scheme until 2016.
Business lobbying group the Confederation of British Industry has called for urgent action to halt the exodus of firms from the London Stock Exchange.
It said that lighter regulation, better marketing and incentives for investors were needed to stem the outflow.
The government declined to say if stock market reform would be part of its Budget this month.
"As has always been the case, decisions on tax are a matter for the chancellor to set out at fiscal events, rather than routinely commenting on rumour, speculation or proposals," a spokesman said.

title: Hedgehog among four chosen animals to feature on new banknotes
summary: The decision comes after nearly half a million people cast their votes from a shortlist of 18 creatures.
body:
Banknotes are getting a nature makeover - and the Bank of England has revealed the four creatures that will feature on our money.
The Atlantic puffin, barn owl, buff-tailed bumblebee and European hedgehog will appear on the redesigned notes in years to come - although no decision has been made about which animal will be shown on which banknote.
The owl, bumblebee and hedgehog topped a public vote in their specific categories, and the puffin was included to celebrate marine life, the coastline and bring variety to the notes, the Bank said.
Wildlife is replacing notable figures from history, such as Sir Winston Churchill, on our cash in a decision that angered a number of leading politicians.
"We have chosen four distinct and inspiring animals that not only showcase the great variety of wildlife we have in the UK but will also enhance the security of our banknotes," said Victoria Cleland, the Bank's chief cashier.
A panel of wildlife experts drew up a shortlist of 18 mammals, birds, amphibians insects and fish which wereput forward to public nominations. Respondents were invited to select up to six.
More than 2.5 million votes were cast by 478,531 people, ranging from wildlife enthusiasts to primary school classes.
The buff-tailed bumblebee (Bombus terrestris) was a clear winner, receiving 360,399 votes, nearly 90,000 more than the barn owl (Tyto alba).
The European hedgehog (Erinaceus europaeus) was most popular in the mammals category.
The red fox, in the mammals category, and the common kingfisher, among the birds, received more nominations than the Atlantic puffin. The puffin (Fratercula arctica) was still selected because it was the most popular marine animal.
The Bank said its inclusion added variety to the series, made the denominations easier to distinguish, and gave an opportunity to celebrate the British coastline.
The puffin and bees also feature on coins, as part of theRoyal Mint's redesigned 20p and £1 coins respectively.
Mock-ups of the new Bank of England banknotes featuring all four winners
Each of the quartet of creatures will feature as the central image of a £5, £10, £20 or £50 note, which will also feature other elements from nature as part of their designs, potentially including other shortlisted animals. The monarch will still feature on the other side of the notes.
Rhys Phillips, the Bank's incoming chief cashier who will be responsible for the roll-out of the new series of notes, said the process of designing, testing and printing banknotes could take years.
He said the Bank needed to make sure they were high-quality, resilient and accessible. As the designs were only in the very early stages, they would be unveiled closer to their launch.
"We'll now work to design, test and produce the banknotes, combining the imagery we've announced today with cutting-edge security features and materials science," he said.
Wildlife already appears on banknotes in the UK, with mackerel, otters, red squirrels and osprey featuring onnotes issued by the Royal Bank of Scotland,external.
Churchill's granddaughter happy with his picture being replaced on the £5 note
Yet it will be the first time since 1970 that the reverse side of Bank of England notes will no longer feature notable figures from history.
On notes circulating currently, in ascending order of value, are former Prime Minister Sir Winston Churchill, author Jane Austen, artist JMW Turner and mathematician and wartime codebreaker Alan Turing.
The proposed removal of wartime leader Churchill angered Reform leader Nigel Farage, and Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey, with Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch describing the move as "a silly thing to do".
The Bank said the move was primarily to stop counterfeiting so all images needed to be replaced on banknotes over time.

title: We spent thousands on a Tui river cruise but ended up on coach trips
summary: Passengers have described their anger after their itineraries changed to involve hours spent on coach trips instead.
body:
Richard Pearson says he barely got to experience any river cruising on his holiday, but spent hours on coaches
Passengers who paid thousands of pounds for European river cruises with Tui have described their anger after their itineraries changed to involve hours spent on coach trips instead.
Several have told the BBC they believe they should get some money back, but have been offered no refund.
Tui apologised and blamed low water levels on the Danube, adding that customers continued their holidays on amended itineraries under its standard booking conditions.
It follows previous complaints aboutconditions on board two of Tui's river vessels.
Richard Pearson took this photo of one of the coach journeys he had not expected as part of his river cruise
Those who contacted the BBC include Richard Pearson from Lincolnshire, whose week-long holiday began on 21 September.
Upon arrival in Budapest, he says passengers were told their vessel, Isla, was in Vienna and could not get to them, so they were being put up in a hotel instead, which he describes as "average".
The next day involved a four-hour coach journey to reach the ship.
The vessel then sailed overnight - meaning no chance to take in the scenery - to Krems. It then stayed there for a few days, with passengers bussed on day trips to locations between 45 minutes and two hours away. The return sailing to Vienna was also in the dark.
The one time there was a "scenic sail" during the day, it was a round trip back to Krems which started early in the morning.
Richard says the food and the staff on board Isla were excellent, but overall the experience was not what he expected when he booked the trip - especially the schedule.
He worked out that "we spent 14 to 15 hours of that holiday on a coach trip, plus time wasted waiting for coaches".
Richard says the reason people were given for the changes of plan was "circumstances beyond [Tui's] control because of the low water levels".
"[But] the main thing for us was it wasn't relaxing. It wasn't a river cruise, it was a little bit of sailing, a floating hotel with coach transfers."
If they had been offered a refund, Richard and his partner would have not gone.
He is now contacting Tui to complain and request some of their £3,300 back.
Sue Crosby says she and her husband didn't want to go on a tour on coaches every day
Sue Crosby and her husband booked on Isla, with the holiday starting on 14 September - her 70th birthday.
She had a similar experience and told the BBC: "We feel as though we've been had."
A revised itinerary was sent a few days before departure, making clear there would be multiple coach trips on offer due to low water levels on the Danube.
The couple didn't want to do this and so asked for a refund. But after being told no refund was possible, they travelled "reluctantly".
Sue Crosby says there was significantly less river cruising time on her holiday than expected when she booked
Even during the trip, the schedule changed further.
It wasn't the river levels themselves that frustrated Sue. "It's how they handled it, and the fact they're still advertising the holidays now."
She also describes the food and the people on the ship as great. However, her complaint is "about the drastic change of itinerary... and the fact we weren't able to get a full refund".
Sue says there were only two half days of sailing where people could actually experience a river cruise.
"We didn't want to go on a tour on coaches every day."
David Mallon and a group of five others were due to travel on 21 September. But they decided the new itinerary presented to them a few days before departure was so different from what they had booked that they didn't want to go.
"What they were planning to give us was not a cruise but a glorified coach trip," says David.
One reason for not wanting to accept the new plan was that a member of the group was meant to be avoiding long periods of sitting down - such as coach journeys - for health reasons.
With no offer of a refund, the group booked a last-minute holiday to Kos instead and decided to try and claim money back on their return.
"We don't blame Tui for the water levels, but it's the way they've handled the consequences of that," David says.
He has now submitted a complaint to Tui and says he will take his quest for a refund to the small claims court if necessary.
The BBC contacted Tui River Cruises about passengers' unhappiness with the extensive itinerary changes and the fact they were not offered any refund.
In a statement, a spokesperson said: "Extreme heat across Europe this summer caused low water levels on the Danube, affecting river cruise operators across the region. We review every sailing individually with our nautical partners.
"Customers on the Tui Isla departures on 14 and 21 September were sent revised itineraries before travelling. Where the ship couldn't sail sections of the river, we arranged coach transfers, hotel stays and adjusted travel arrangements to minimise transfer times so customers could still visit destinations, including Budapest, Vienna and Bratislava.
"We reviewed the revised arrangements carefully and customers continued their holiday on the amended itinerary under our standard booking conditions. While customers were still able to visit the key destinations on their itinerary, we're sorry some did not get the river cruise experience they had anticipated."

title: Boots sold in £7bn deal to Canadian billionaire family
summary: The sale of the High Street chain was announced on Wednesday.
body:
Boots, the High Street pharmacy and retail chain, has been sold in an $8.9bn (£6.7bn) deal to Canada's billionaire Weston family.
Wittington Investments, the holding company, confirmed it had agreed to buy the 177-year-old retailer on Wednesday from US private equity firm Sycamore Partners and the Pessina family.
Boots started as a simple apothecary in Nottingham but has evolved to become a stalwart of the High Street, expanding its business to sell a vast range of health and beauty products, meal deals and travel accessories.
The chain has performed well in recent years despite challenges from rivals and changing shopping habits.
Its stores have seen lower footfall as people switched to working from home rather than visiting town and city centre offices every weekday.
It has closed hundreds of branches across the UK in recent years, leaving it with about 1,800 stores and 51,000 employees, but remains a familiar British brand.
In its most recent annual results, Boots generated £7.5bn in sales - a 3.2% increase on 2024.
Retail expert Catherine Shuttleworth, chief executive of savvy marketing, said shoppers were unlikely to see much change to stores in the coming months, but added what they can "expect over time is an improved shopping experience as the new owners invest in the business".
She said health and beauty was a "massive area for growth", and fresh investment from its new ownership would help.
The last two decades has seen several changes of ownership under discussion and sometimes completed.
Sycamore only owned the retailer for 18 months, and Shuttleworth said the chopping and changing of owners had been "an unhelpful distraction".
Boots gets new US owner in multi-billion dollar deal
The company was established by John Boot, who opened the first herbalist store in Nottingham, offering an affordable alternative to traditional medicines in 1849.
It has since expanded over the decades into selling various products, but health products have remained a key part of its business.
As well as vaccines, it offers eye and hearing tests, providing much needed health care support in everyday moments as well as at times of national crisis like the coronavirus pandemic.
It launched its loyalty scheme in 1997, the Advantage Card, which became hugely popular and a move repeated by various retailers since.
Galen Weston, the chairman of Wittington, will become chairman of Boots.
He signalled the new owners had fresh plans for the chain, including shop upgrades and an expansion of healthcare services.
"We see a meaningful opportunity to make a great business even better through stable long-term ownership, further capital investment, and the renewed operating focus required to serve customers with excellence for generations to come," he said.
The Weston family will be buying Boots' retail operations in the UK and Ireland, Boots Opticians, No7 Beauty Company and its Thailand and franchised businesses. It is set be completed in early 2027.
The Weston family owns the Canadian grocery chain Loblaws, pharmacy business Shoppers Drug Mart, and previously owned the London department store Selfridges from 2003 to 2021, before selling it for $4bn.
The separate UK branch of the Weston family is the majority owner of Associated British Foods, the parent firm of Primark.
The Westons were ranked fifth on this year's Sunday Times Rich List with a combined fortune of almost £19bn.
Wittington will have operational control over Boots, it has secured ownership in partnership with Fairfax Financial Holdings, a Toronto-based holding company.
Sycamore Partners, in partnership with Stefano Pessina and his family, will retain ownership of The Boots Group's Farmacias Benavides in Mexico and Alliance Healthcare Deutschland in Germany.

title: OpenAI says teen ChatGPT use limited but research finds it an 'unacceptable risk'
summary: The research found that important guardrails for teens using ChatGPT often failed.
body:
Young people's use of internet platforms like ChatGPT has come under increased scrutiny.
OpenAI's ChatGPT for Teens was designed to promote healthier use of the artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot, but new research has found its important safety features fall short.
The major AI firm rolled out many teen safety guardrails in August, including curbs on emotional dependence and new parental alerts for problematic use.
On Wednesday, OpenAI said it found average teen use of ChatGPT to be relatively limited and tended toward "learning" activity.
However, research released the same day from non-profit Common Sense Media found that ChatGPT still poses an "unacceptable risk" for teens as safety features, including notifying parents of self-harm conversations, often fail.
When OpenAI this summer released what it calledChatGPT for Teens,external, it said users identified as being between the ages of 13 and 17 would be opted into "features to promote healthy use and additional controls for parents".
Those features include preventing teen ChatGPT users from engaging in romantic or other language that could encourage " emotional dependence," including preventing the tool from implying that it was in any way conscious. There are also blocks on sexualized imagery and "reminders" for teens if they were to share an image that was "sensitive."
The features are also meant to enable parents to receive notifications, if they had linked to their children's ChatGPT account, about chats that included discussions of self-harm or disordered eating.
OpenAI said those features have caused an uptick in teen use focused on learning, from study help to advice on their school work.
In addition to seeing the average teen user on ChatGPT for less than 15 minutes a day, OpenAI said that for longer stretches of use, automatic reminders to take a break work well. Almost half of teen users quickly stopped using ChatGPT after such a reminder.
The company added that, for teens who are seen to have used ChatGPT for three consecutive hours or more, their prompts included something related to learning in more than 80% of such cases.
But Common Sense Media'snew research,externaldetermined that ChatGPT for Teens was an "unacceptable risk" for young people and parents, and said OpenAI should ban people under 18 years old from using the platform until teen guardrails were proven reliable.
An OpenAI spokesman said a review of Common Sense Media's methodology found that much of the testing may have begun and concluded before activation of parental controls was complete."
"We welcome rigorous independent evaluation, but we do not believe Common Sense Media's testing accurately reflects how ChatGPT's teen safeguards work in practice or expert perspectives on how AI can support teens," he said.
While the firm's research, done through multiple accounts registered as belonging to a teen and conversations before and after the teen guardrails were put in place, found that ChatGPT was good at avoiding "sexual roleplay" with young users, other OpenAI guardrails failed, including for discussions of suicide.
The research found that even an hour of teen-ChatGPT conversation about "suicidal ideation, self-harm, or disordered eating on newly created, parent-linked accounts" resulted in "zero" alerts sent to parents.
It was only older ChatGPT accounts with "weeks of accumulated conversation history on sensitive topics" that would result in a parental alert.
In such conversations, ChatGPT also "failed to reliably recommend that teens in crisis connect to a hotline or professional," the report found.
The tests also showed that ChatGPT for Teens continues to do school work, and that the bot still will engage in anthropomorphised language or "talk like it's a friend," despite OpenAI's promise to curb that behaviour.
"ChatGPT for Teens could give parents false confidence in guardrails and safety alerts that frequently don't work," Tom Siegel, who leads the Youth AI Safety Institute within Common Sense, said.
The way young people interact with online platforms has become a major issue in recent years as self-harm and suicide among children has become more common.
This year has seen several lawsuits looking to hold companieslike Meta,TikTokandothersresponsible for harming the mental health of children end in unprecedented losses for the firms.
OpenAI, too, has come under increased scrutiny and legal pressure over the way young people use ChatGPT.
The Tumbler Ridge mass shooting in rural Canada in February was carried out by an 18-year old who had for months prior been discussing gun violence with ChatGPT.
OpenAI has previously apologised for failing to flag the shooter's account with law enforcement, and is facingseveral lawsuitsover the incident.

title: Burnham to hold security talks with German chancellor in Berlin
summary: Downing Street said deeper co-operation in the face of rising hybrid threats from Russia would be high on the agenda during Burnham's first official visit to Germany.
body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham will meet his German counterpart Friedrich Merz in Berlin on Friday
Prime Minister Andy Burnham will hold talks on tackling cyber-security threats and sabotage with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Thursday.
Downing Street said deeper co-operation in the face of rising hybrid threats from Russia would be high on the agenda during Burnham's first official visit to Germany.
Intelligence services in both countries have warned of rising threats, including last month when Germany accused Russia oflaunching a drone fitted with explosives at Leipzig/Halle Airport.
The Berlin talks come days after Burnham told the Labour Party's conference he wanted to set out options for a closer relationship with the EU later this year, including the prospect of eventually rejoining the bloc.
A German government spokesman has said any future in-out referendum would be primarily a question for Britain, but that Berlin supports stronger ties between the UK and the EU.
Burnham is set to be greeted with military honours at the German capital's Chancellery ahead of his first face-to-face meeting with the chancellor.
On Thursday, the two leaders will formally ratify the 2025 Kensington Treaty, a partnership committing both countries to tackle hostile activity through deeper cooperation on science, technology, defence, security and growth.
Speaking ahead of the visit, Burnham said the UK and Germany were "joining forces to find, expose and disrupt" threats.
He continued: "Attacks on our infrastructure, our businesses and our democracies are not a distant threat.
"They reach into people's homes and workplaces, and they are designed to make us weaker and more divided."
The talks come during a period in which Merz's own political future has come under intense scrutiny.
Burnham replaced Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer in July after the former leader was forced out by his own MPs just two years after winning a landslide election victory.
Similarly, Merz has faced persistent rumours he could be replaced by his party due to his poor approval ratings and followingsetbacks in regional elections.
Although the chancellor appears to have overcome an immediate crisis in his leadership, questions remain over his future.
The security talks also come in a week when questions have been raised about Germany's reliability as an intelligence partner, following the bombshell arrest of a formerspy chief on suspicion of espionage.
August Hanning has been accused of espionage, treason and obtaining classified information for a foreign power, the German Federal Prosecutor's Office says.
He ran the Federal Intelligence Service (BND) from 1998 to 2005 and has since been working as a private consultant.
